e: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads over the AWS edge network to the single destination bucket, and multipart upload parallelizes large transfers. It needs no extra infrastructure. B and C add replication hops or shipping devices, and D adds EC2/EBS snapshot handling, all of which increase operational complexity.

Athena queries JSON data in place in S3 using standard SQL. It is serverless, pay-per-query, and needs no data movement, which fits simple on-demand queries with the least overhead. Redshift, CloudWatch Logs migration, or a transient EMR cluster all require more setup and management.

The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key limits access to principals from any account in the organization. New accounts are covered automatically, so no ongoing maintenance is needed. PrincipalOrgPaths, CloudTrail-driven updates, or per-user tags all need continuous administration.

A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 gives private connectivity from the VPC to S3 without an internet gateway or NAT, at no extra cost. An instance profile controls permissions, not network path. CloudWatch Logs export and API Gateway private link are not valid ways to reach S3 privately.

EBS volumes are tied to one instance and AZ, so each server holds only part of the documents. Amazon EFS is a shared file system that is accessible from multiple instances and AZs, so all servers see all documents. Copying data between EBS volumes would drift immediately, and an ALB cannot split a request across servers to merge their data.

70 TB must be moved as fast as possible while using minimal network bandwidth. Snowball Edge moves the data offline by physical shipping. CLI over the internet, or File Gateway even over Direct Connect, would take a very long time and consume bandwidth.

SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues decouples producers from dozens of consumers, and both services scale to very high throughput. A single Kinesis shard supports only 1,000 records/s of writes. Kinesis Data Analytics is not a message store, and EC2 Auto Scaling on CPU does not decouple the system.

Putting jobs in an SQS queue decouples the coordinator from workers and removes the single primary server. Scaling the Auto Scaling group on queue size matches capacity to variable workload. Scheduled scaling cannot follow variable demand, and CloudTrail or EventBridge are not job queues.

An S3 File Gateway presents an SMB interface on premises with a local cache for recently accessed files (low latency), while data is stored in S3. A lifecycle policy then moves older files to a cheaper class. DataSync alone, FSx alone, or client utilities do not provide cached low-latency access plus lifecycle management.

An SQS FIFO queue preserves message order and provides exactly-once processing, and it can trigger Lambda. SNS and standard SQS queues do not guarantee ordering, and an API Gateway authorizer is for authentication, not for serializing orders.

Secrets Manager stores database credentials centrally and has built-in automatic rotation for Aurora, which minimizes operational effort. Parameter Store has no native automatic rotation. Storing credentials in S3 or on encrypted EBS volumes leaves rotation manual.

A single CloudFront distribution with both the S3 bucket (static) and the ALB (dynamic) as origins caches static content at the edge and accelerates dynamic content over the AWS backbone. Route 53 can alias the domain to it. Global Accelerator cannot use S3 as an endpoint, and the other options add needless complexity.

Secrets Manager supports scheduled rotation for RDS and multi-Region secret replication, so it covers cross-Region rotation with minimal effort. Parameter Store does not rotate secrets or replicate across Regions natively. S3 or DynamoDB with custom Lambda code means much more to build and maintain.

Aurora with Multi-AZ gives high availability, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes Aurora Replicas as read load changes, which fits an unpredictable read-heavy workload with MySQL compatibility. Redshift is for analytics, a Single-AZ RDS deployment is not highly available, and Memcached does not replace the database.

AWS Network Firewall is a managed stateful firewall with intrusion prevention for VPC traffic, supporting custom rules for inspection and filtering. GuardDuty only detects threats, Traffic Mirroring only copies traffic for analysis, and Firewall Manager centrally manages rules but does not itself inspect traffic.

QuickSight can connect to both S3 and RDS PostgreSQL, and dashboards are shared with QuickSight users and groups (management gets full access, others limited). QuickSight sharing is not done through IAM roles. Glue/Athena options do not provide visualization or fine-grained dashboard sharing.

EC2 instances receive AWS permissions through an IAM role (via an instance profile), which supplies temporary credentials automatically. Policies, groups, and users cannot be attached to an instance directly, and long-term user keys on instances are an anti-pattern.

S3 event notifications to an SQS queue and a Lambda function using the queue as its event source form a durable, stateless pipeline; the message is deleted after successful processing, so failures are retried. Keeping state in Lambda memory or on an EC2 instance is neither durable nor stateless, and an email alert is not automatic processing.

Gateway Load Balancer is designed to insert third-party virtual appliances transparently in the traffic path. A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint sends traffic to the appliance in the inspection VPC and returns it, with least operational overhead. NLB/ALB are not transparent inspection insertion points, and a transit gateway alone does not inspect packets.

Snapshots restored to new EBS volumes create independent copies, so test changes don't affect production. Fast snapshot restore makes restored volumes fully initialized at creation, giving consistent high I/O immediately and minimizing clone time. Instance store cannot be restored from snapshots, and Multi-Attach would share the same production volume.

S3 plus CloudFront for static content, with API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB for the backend, is fully serverless, scales to millions of requests with millisecond latency, and has the least operational overhead. EC2/EKS options require capacity and cluster management, and storing orders in S3 does not fit transactional data.

Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers for unpredictable access with no retrieval fees, and stores data across multiple AZs. Standard costs more for rarely used files, Standard-IA charges retrieval fees, and One Zone-IA does not survive loss of an AZ.

Files are not accessed after one month but must be kept indefinitely, so Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage. A lifecycle rule moves them there after 1 month. Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, and One Zone-IA are all more expensive for data that is effectively never read.

Cost Explorer provides built-in graphs and filters/grouping by instance type over a selectable period, so it needs no setup and can show the last 2 months and the root cause. Budgets are for alerting, the Billing dashboard is not granular enough, and CUR with QuickSight requires much more setup.

Decoupling ingestion from database loading with an SQS queue buffers bursts and lets the loader Lambda consume at a controlled rate, improving scalability with minimal configuration. SNS does not buffer or retry like a queue. Rewriting to Tomcat on EC2 or switching to DynamoDB with DAX adds heavy effort.

AWS Config continuously records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules, so it detects unauthorized configuration changes to S3 buckets. Trusted Advisor gives periodic best-practice checks, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and access logging records requests, not configuration changes.
